item.title: Statistical analysis of crossing beam speckle fields
item.description: arXiv:2611.33483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building on the statistical analysis of single beam speckles, this paper develops a statistical description of speckle fields formed by crossing laser beams. A formal definition of individual speckles and their domains allows us to quantify the effective size and abundance of speckles. For two crossing beams, the effective speckle size is derived from the local curvature of the intensity field, and the expected speckle abundance is found asymptotically with the Kac-Rice formula. Monte Carlo simulations of speckle abundance show excellent agreement with the theoretical abundance formula. The two beam speckle analysis is then applied to a symmetric quad beam configuration motivated by polarization smoothing and demonstrates that increasing the separation between beams reduces expected stimulated Brillouin scattering reflectivity from saturated speckles. The statistical model is then extended to an arbitrary number of beams using a coordinate free formulation to obtain the spectral density of laser driven electron density fluctuations.
item.dc:creator: Ian D. Min-Roberts, Wojciech Rozmus, Pierre A. Michel

item.title: Deep-learning-enabled rapid spatially multiplexed wavefront sensing with a thin diffuser
item.description: arXiv:2611.33724v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional wavefront sensing typically measures aberrations along a single guide-star direction, limiting the correction of field-dependent aberrations over a wide field of view. Spatial multiplexing with a thin diffuser enables simultaneous measurements across multiple isoplanatic patches, but the computational cost of reconstruction makes it difficult to track changing aberrations. We propose a deep-learning approach that combines recurrent all-pairs field transforms for displacement estimation with Zernike coefficient regression. Experimental results show that the method accurately reconstructs multiple wavefronts from a single speckle pattern and reduces three-channel reconstruction time from 2801.6 ms with conventional digital image correlation (DIC) to 23.1 ms. The reconstructed wavefronts agreed more closely with sequential single-channel references than those obtained by multiplexed DIC, and simulations showed that Zernike regression was more robust to noise than direct gradient integration. These results suggest a path toward dynamic wide-field aberration sensing and high-speed adaptive optics.
item.dc:creator: Ming Xue, Shijie Wei, Shulei Zhao, Zhuojia Shi, Tengfei Wu, Xiaopeng Shao

item.title: Carrier relaxation confines the Bogdanov--Takens degeneracy of an optically injected semiconductor laser
item.description: arXiv:2611.33746v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optically injected semiconductor lasers are forced nonlinear oscillators whose locking boundaries are organized by codimension-two points. We ask which property of the carrier balance permits or forbids a Bogdanov--Takens (BT) point in the standard three-dimensional rate equations. Taking the carrier inversion $n$ as distinguished observable, the rate that enters the spectral conditions is the slope of the gain--loss balance, $\xi=\partial\dot n/\partial n=-2\Gamma/\kappa$, where $\Gamma$ is the damping of the relaxation oscillation and $\kappa=1+2Bn$ the normalized stimulated-emission factor. The two BT conditions become affine in $\xi$ and imply the exact sum rule $K^{2}=I[1-(1+\kappa)I]$ between injection amplitude $K$ and intracavity intensity $I$. The product of the two relaxation eigenvalues that survive at a saddle-node is bounded below by $1-16\Gamma^{2}$, so that no BT point exists for $\Gamma<1/4$, whatever $B$, the linewidth enhancement factor, the injection strength and the detuning; below this barrier every contact between Hopf and saddle-node curves is a fold--Hopf point. For $B=0$ the barrier is completed to an exact existence criterion. We prove that the unfolding of a BT point by injection strength and detuning is transversal if and only if two explicit curves cross transversally in the plane of locked states; for $B=0$ this is a simple root of an explicit function, and transversality fails exactly at the existence threshold. Two BT points at $\Gamma=1/2$, $\alpha=2$ are verified to be generic, and the contacts between Hopf and saddle-node curves are classified into fold--Hopf, BT and nilpotent triple-zero points.
item.dc:creator: A. Mart\'in-Ruiz, E. Chan-L\'opez, Carlos Antonio Mar\'in-Mendoza

item.title: Existence of single-resonance parametric bound states in the continuum: System of Schr\"odinger equations
item.description: arXiv:2611.33784v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A bound state in the continuum (BIC) is an eigenmode of a linear wave system with its eigen-frequency embedded in the radiation continuum of scattering states. At the frequency of a BIC, scattering problems with given incident waves from infinity lose uniqueness. Due to their close connection with strong resonance effects, BICs have found many useful applications in classical and quantum wave systems. Existence theories of BICs have been established for some cases involving the so-called symmetry-protected BICs, Friedrich-Wintgen BICs, and Fabry-Perot BICs. The single-resonance parametric BICs (srp-BICs) are another important class of BICs. Such a BIC emerges from a single resonant state through tuning a real parameter. Using a simple system of two one-dimensional Schr\"odinger equations, we demonstrate the formation of srp-BICs and establish a rigorous existence theory.
item.dc:creator: Xiuchen Yu, Ya Yan Lu

item.title: Transport Layer-Driven Optimization of Color and Efficiency in TADF OLEDs for Large-Area Applications
item.description: arXiv:2611.33933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Balancing structural simplicity with high efficiency is crucial for practical applications of organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs), especially in large-area lighting devices. Optimizing the charge-transport layers in multilayer OLEDs controls the recombination zone within the emissive layer, thereby enhancing the device's performance. Herein, we experimentally and computationally investigate how the thicknesses of the electron and hole transport layers affect the performance of orange-red thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) OLEDs. Using a TADF emitter, 2-[4-(diphenylamino)phenyl]-10,10-dioxide-9H-thioxanthen-9-one (TXO-TPA), at 10 wt\% concentration in 4,4-Bis(N-carbazolyl)-1,1-biphenyl (CBP) host, we achieve a maximum external quantum efficiency ($\eta_{EQE}$) of 20.86\% and a peak luminance of 32,800 cd m$^{-2}$. Using a combination of drift-diffusion and optical simulations, we reveal how variations in hole- and electron-transport-layer thicknesses modulate the charge-carrier balance and shift the recombination zone within the emissive layer. This tuning not only optimizes exciton formation but also enables color tuning from green to red without altering the emissive material. Our findings highlight the critical role of transport layer engineering in achieving efficient, color-controlled OLEDs with simplified architectures. Furthermore, we successfully demonstrate a large-area OLED device (~20 cm$^{2}$), achieving an impressive $\eta_{EQE}$ of 17\%, underscoring the scalability and practicality of our approach for general lighting applications.
item.dc:creator: Manish Kumar, Jawid Nikan, Luiz Pereira

item.title: Ferroionic CuCrP2S6 Integrated Silicon Photonics for Neuromorphic Computing
item.description: arXiv:2611.33954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neuromorphic photonic computing calls for optical states that combine stimulus accumulation, spontaneous relaxation, and nonvolatile state retention without continuous power dissipation. Here, we demonstrate a ferroionic photonic platform by integrating layered van der Waals CuCrP2S6 onto silicon microring resonators using a back-end integration process. Electrical pulsing produces unidirectional blue shifts in the optical resonance, consistent with field-driven redistribution of mobile Cu ions and giving rise to a history-dependent optical response. The resulting optical state is strongly pulse dependent, exhibiting both volatile and nonvolatile components. A short 20-pulse excitation produces an initial 70 pm resonance shift that relaxes toward baseline within approximately 60 s, with a volatile relaxation time constant of 27-29 s. In contrast, after 1000 pulses, an initial 0.27 nm resonance shift relaxes to a persistent 0.13 nm nonvolatile state that is retained for at least 24 h. Repeated 6 V electrical pulses produce a progressive resonance shift over 1000 cycles, demonstrating cumulative optical integration. A fixed-wavelength readout converts the accumulated resonance shift into a thresholded optical response, with the normalized transmission remaining above the selected threshold through 600 pulses and falling below it at the 800-pulse state. These dynamics realize the basis for a leaky integrate-and-fire photonic neuron, where the pulse-dependent ionic response provides integration, spontaneous relaxation supplies a passive leak, persistent states provide nonvolatile memory, and fixed-wavelength readout provides an optical threshold response.
item.dc:creator: Ghada Dushaq, Srinivasa R. Tamalampudi, Mahmoud Rasras

item.title: Gradient Optical Diffraction Tomography Using Deep Learning-Assisted Amplitude Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2611.34059v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gradient Optical Diffraction Tomography (GODT) enables the non-invasive reconstruction of a spatial derivative of the 3D sample's refractive index distribution, providing enhanced sensitivity to subtle refractive index variations through gradient-based contrast. Implemented using lateral shearing interferometry (LSI), GODT benefits from a common-path architecture that provides environmental stability and high signal-to-noise ratio measurements. Unlike conventional optical diffraction tomography (ODT), which requires numerical integration of LSI-derived phase gradients to recover the object phase, GODT enables direct tomographic reconstruction from the LSI data. Notably, GODT requires derivatives of both the phase and amplitude of the object fields as input. While the phase derivative can be readily extracted from LSI data, the amplitude gradient cannot be directly retrieved. Thus, in the original GODT formulation, the amplitude gradient was assumed to be negligible, limiting the accuracy of the resulting 3D reconstruction. In this work, we introduce amplitude-informed GODT (AI-GODT), which employs physics-informed supervised deep learning to estimate the missing amplitude gradient based on accessible LSI data, specifically the fringe modulation. The proposed approach, applying a ResNet architecture and training on computer-generated data, is validated through numerical simulation and experimental measurements of both a well-characterized test object and primary neuronal cell culture, demonstrating the network's ability to generalize to diverse samples. We show that incorporation of the recovered amplitude gradient into the GODT reconstruction pipeline improves the 3D reconstruction quality, especially in its out-of-focus regions. The software and datasets are openly available to facilitate reproducibility and further development.
item.dc:creator: Julianna Winnik (Institute of Micromechanics and Photonics, Warsaw University of Technology, Warsaw, Poland), Piotr Zda\'nkowski (Institute of Micromechanics and Photonics, Warsaw University of Technology, Warsaw, Poland), Konrad Kosuge (Institute of Micromechanics and Photonics, Warsaw University of Technology, Warsaw, Poland), Aleksandra Parys (Institute of Micromechanics and Photonics, Warsaw University of Technology, Warsaw, Poland), Marzena Stefaniuk (Laboratory of Neurobiology, BRAINCITY, Nencki Institute of Experimental Biology, Polish Academy of Sciences, Warsaw, Poland), Junwei Min (State Key Laboratory of Ultrafast Optical Science and Technology, Xi'an Institute of Optics and Precision Mechanics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Xi'an, China), Baoli Yao (State Key Laboratory of Ultrafast Optical Science and Technology, Xi'an Institute of Optics and Precision Mechanics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Xi'an, China, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China), Maciej Trusiak (Institute of Micromechanics and Photonics, Warsaw University of Technology, Warsaw, Poland)

item.title: Minimum Effective-Susceptibility Bounds for Arbitrary Polarization Transformations in Metasurfaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.34146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metasurfaces are increasingly employed for sophisticated polarization transformations, including general unitary and nonunitary Jones operations. Despite substantial advances in analytical synthesis methods, inverse design of these transformations remains challenging. Here, we show that the particular mathematical structure of Jones polarization transformations makes optimal effective-susceptibility synthesis analytically tractable within the generalized sheet transition condition (GSTC) framework. For reciprocal, lossless dipolar metasurfaces, we establish exact feasibility and global minimum attainment, and derive sharp effective-susceptibility bounds for representative unitary and nonunitary transformations. We identify when magnetoelectric coupling lowers the minimum susceptibility, when it offers no resource advantage, and how the required material response depends on the prescribed polarization transformation. Applications to polarization rotations, tunable compensators, and polarization-state separation, including unambiguous discrimination, demonstrate sharp physical limits and material-resource trade-offs. These results provide geometry-independent theoretical benchmarks that can guide numerical inverse design and the selection of metasurface architectures.
item.dc:creator: Ravi Hegde

item.title: Fourier-Transform Photothermal Spectroscopy with Transient-Lens Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.34361v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate Fourier-transform photothermal spectroscopy using broadband supercontinuum excitation and transient-lens detection. The output of a Ti:sapphire oscillator is broadened in a photonic crystal fiber to generate the supercontinuum pump, which is converted into a phase-stable pulse pair with a controllable femtosecond delay using a birefringent interferometer. The absorption-induced heating from the pump generates a transient thermal lens in the sample, which is detected as a function of delay by an off-resonant 800 nm photothermal probe beam. Fourier transform of the interferometric photothermal response yields a frequency-domain signal corresponding to the sample absorptance spectrum weighted by the pump spectrum. After division by the measured pump spectrum, the reconstructed photothermal spectrum is compared with a direct frequency-domain linear absorption measurement to evaluate the accuracy of the reconstruction. This method combines Fourier-transform broadband excitation with thermal-lens readout, allowing broadband linear absorption spectra to be obtained from pump-induced refractive-index changes rather than from transmitted excitation intensity. We demonstrate the method on phloxine B.
item.dc:creator: Asha S. Thomas, Toluwatomi Haastrup, Luzhou Yu, Muyi Zhang, Jennifer P. Ogilvie

item.title: Unveiling gauge-invariant on-chip phases from light intensity
item.description: arXiv:2611.34384v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-informed digital twins fitted to output powers increasingly program photonic processors, but these powers do not fix the implemented phase, which determines how light from different inputs interferes. Here we show that a twin trained on intensities alone predicts the gauge-invariant phase of programmed transformations, and that this prediction can be used to program the phase. On a $12\times12$ mesh, with phases measured by interference protocols formed by the mesh itself, intensity-only and phase-aware programs from random starts reach the same intensity fidelity but phase fidelities of 0.690 and 0.996, both as predicted by the twin. The prediction holds for blocks up to $10\times10$. With coherent inputs, the programmed phase determines the outputs: phase-aware programming reduces the direction-of-arrival error of an on-chip Butler matrix from 29 degrees to 2.0 degrees. Power measurements alone thus yield a phase-calibrated model of the mesh, without phase data in training or optics beyond the chip.
item.dc:creator: Huiwen Li, Andrea Cataldo, Rohan Yadgirkar, Jun Gao, Ali W. Elshaari

item.title: Producing and Measuring Circularly Polarized X-rays: A Jones and Mueller-Stokes Treatment of Crystal Phase Plates
item.description: arXiv:2611.34391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Converting a linearly polarized X-ray beam into a circularly polarized one, and then verifying the polarization state actually delivered, are standard operations at synchrotron radiation facilities. The key optical element is a quarter-wave plate (QWP), a birefringent crystal that introduces a 90-degree (quarter-wavelength) phase retardation between the two orthogonal components of the electric field. This paper presents a self-contained theoretical treatment of X-ray polarization optics. We first establish the Jones and Mueller-Stokes formalisms and their connection via the Pauli matrices, fixing the sign and handedness conventions explicitly and reconciling them with those used elsewhere in the literature. From there we derive the Jones and Mueller matrices of a general retarder at an arbitrary orientation angle chi (including the QWP that converts horizontal linear polarization into circular polarization of either handedness) and of linear polarizers, and describe the experimental Stokes polarimetry protocol used at synchrotron beamlines. These results are then combined to treat the general crystal phase plate, characterized by two complex reflection (or transmission) amplitudes r_s and r_p, obtaining the degree of circular polarization delivered for an arbitrary incident beam as a function of chi and the phase retardation delta. Finally, we turn to the practical implementation of these elements with perfect-crystal diffraction: the residual polarization impurity of a Brewster-angle polarizer and the role of ray tracing in evaluating it, and the choice of diffraction geometry (Bragg or Laue, diffracted or transmitted beam) for obtaining a significant, controllable phase shift. The formalism presented here is the mathematical background of the treatment of polarization in the ray-tracing code SHADOW4.
item.dc:creator: Manuel Sanchez del Rio, Carsten Detlefs

item.title: Solitons as conversion events in quadratic crystals
item.description: arXiv:2611.34454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a $\chi^{(2)}$ crystal with temporal walk-off and negligible dispersion, signal, idler and pump pulses obey the integrable three-wave interaction. For a pump of intermediate group velocity we describe each soliton as a conversion event: the fusion of a signal--idler pair into a pump pulse, or the decay of a pump pulse, at a definite depth in the crystal. The asymptotic $\mathrm{sech}$ pulses, usually treated with three separate $2\times2$ scattering problems, are the legs of the event, a single pole of the $3\times3$ problem. For one event we give the conversion curve in closed form and the minimum crystal length; for several events, the rule by which they displace each other. A pump pulse is unstable, and its growing mode is the tail of a decay event: a seed carrying a fraction $\varepsilon$ of the photons along this mode makes the pulse decay after $\Gamma^{-1}\ln(c_+/\varepsilon)$, with $\Gamma$ the conversion rate and $c_+$ of order one. Unmatched signal and idler pulses form the resonance of Kaup, Reiman and Bers; we show that it is a fusion followed by a decay, each within a conversion length, and give its pump photon number in closed form. Since the delay between the input pulses sets the depth of the vertex, these quantities can be read on the output face of a single crystal; we give the scales for periodically poled KTiOPO$_4$.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Beccarini, Claudio Conti

item.title: Arbitrarily Weak Losses Destroy Fractal Bandstructure in Temporal Fibonacci Quasicrystals
item.description: arXiv:2611.34552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lossless photonic crystals with weak refractive index contrasts block limited frequencies. However, the same materials arranged in a non-periodic Fibonacci quasicrystal block all but infinitely rare fractally-distributed frequencies. Similar analysis shows that weak quasiperiodic refractive index variation in time should achieve infinitely broadband gain. We demonstrate that any small experimental losses immediately destroy this effect. Our methods also provide smoothness and approximation theorems for the localisation lengths central to topology in spatial problems.
item.dc:creator: Calvin M. Hooper

item.title: Theory of Observability of Voigt-Wave Propagation in a Homogeneous Dielectric Material
item.description: arXiv:2611.34578v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A Voigt wave can propagate in a dissipative anisotropic dielectric material when a 4$\times$4 propagation matrix is defective, as happens for a uniform plane wave along a singular axis, and the field depends on the propagation distance linearly as well as exponentially. Whether it is observable outside a slab of that material generally depends on whether the defectiveness is inherited by the 2$\times$2 reflection and transmission matrices, which are extracted from the 2$\times$2 blocks of a 4$\times$4 transfer matrix that relates the fields at the two faces of the slab. Explicit tests exist for each type of defectiveness, and a counting argument shows that excitation and observability co-occur at oblique incidence only for isolated combinations of constitutive parameters and slab thickness. Normal incidence is exceptional: Voigt-wave excitation then generally implies a defective transmission matrix for almost all thicknesses, which explains Voigt's 1902 experiment on andalusite. Numerical searches for andalusite, $\beta$-gallium oxide, terbium orthoaluminate in a magnetostatic field, and hexagonal boron nitride show that a Voigt wave may be excited without being observable and that a defective reflection or transmission matrix need not signal the excitation of a Voigt wave.
item.dc:creator: Akhlesh Lakhtakia, Tom G. Mackay

item.title: Tunable Terahertz Bandpass Filter based on the Photonic Emulation of a 2DEG Interferometer through the Geometric Phase of Light
item.description: arXiv:2611.34593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Terahertz frequencies are expected to become a key player in next-generation wireless communications. For this transition to occur seamlessly, tunable bandpass filters for channel selection are essential. However, conventional Fabry-P\'erot cavity-based bandpass filters face inherent limitations. Specifically, their tunability is restricted by physical constraints, such as the maximum achievable mirror separation. In this work, drawing inspiration from electronic interferometers, we demonstrate a continuously tunable bandpass filter operating near 0.3 THz by exploiting the geometric phase of light, the Pancharatnam-Berry phase. Our device incorporates intracavity waveplates for polarization control and is described by a mathematical expression analogous to that of the electronic interferometer governed by the Aharonov-Bohm phase, thereby realizing a photonic analogue. Using custom-designed subwavelength waveplates and cavity mirrors, we achieve a finesse of $\mathcal{F}\approx17$, a quality factor of $Q\approx1.5\times10^{3}$, and a resonance linewidth of $\Delta f_{\mathrm{FWHM}}\approx 200$ MHz. Beyond terahertz communication technology, this system is expected to find applications in fields requiring high frequency resolution, such as spectroscopy.
item.dc:creator: Victor I. Iwanaga, Hiroaki Shirasaka, Shin'ichiro Hayashi, Katsuhiko Miyamoto, Yoshiharu Urata, Kouji Nawata, Jun-ichi Shikata, Norihiko Sekine, Seigo Ohno

item.title: Blind spatially varying PSF estimation for fluorescence microscopy
item.description: arXiv:2611.34607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical aberrations degrade fluorescence microscopy images and measuring the underlying point spread function (PSF) often requires dedicated acquisitions or isolated emitters. Here we introduce DeepBlur, a neural network that estimates spatially varying two-dimensional PSFs directly from single images of biological structures. Trained entirely on physical simulations spanning aberrations, illumination and noise, it adapts to diverse imaging conditions without requiring user-supplied optical parameters. Using a deformable mirror, we acquire 1,290 images and assess blind PSF estimates against independent references. DeepBlur estimates agree closely with these references and improve deconvolution of experimentally aberrated images. Local PSF estimation also enables correction of spatially varying defocus and improves random-illumination super-resolution reconstruction in biological tissue. Available through DeepInv, a napari plugin and a web demonstration, DeepBlur can be readily integrated into computational microscopy workflows.
item.dc:creator: Minh Hai Nguyen, Florian Sarron, Paul Escande, Sylvain Cantaloube, Thomas Mangeat, Pierre Weiss

item.title: A Reconfigurable Four-State Sensor Based on Orthogonal Thermal and Chemical Stimuli
item.description: arXiv:2611.34834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article presents a novel four-state refractive index (RI) sensor based on distinct phases of palladium (Pd) and vanadium dioxide (VO$_2$), controlled by orthogonal thermal and chemical stimuli. This is a numerical, simulation-only study: all results are obtained from two-dimensional finite-element method (FEM) simulations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first reported multi-state reconfigurable RI sensor tuned by external control. VO$_2$ serves as a phase change material (PCM) offering two thermally switchable phases with highly contrasting optical properties, while the hydrogen absorption property of Pd provides two additional phases. Combining these, four operational states are realized: (i) $\alpha$-Pd/low-$T$ VO$_2$; (ii) $\beta$-PdH$_x$/low-$T$ VO$_2$; (iii) $\alpha$-Pd/high-$T$ VO$_2$; and (iv) $\beta$-PdH$_x$/high-$T$ VO$_2$. Thermal crosstalk between Pd and VO$_2$ is mitigated through tungsten (W) doping of VO$_2$. This work further introduces conditional state sensitivity (CSS), a novel figure of merit quantifying the optical contrast between each state transition. The proposed sensor achieves a peak sensitivity of 2871 nm/RIU for the undoped reference configuration and 2798 nm/RIU for the practical W-doped device, together with a peak CSS of 16,872 nm/RIU, establishing it as a multi-state reconfigurable platform with reduced thermal crosstalk and potential applications in industrial safety monitoring and optical logic gates.
item.dc:creator: Ashfaq Ur Rahman Ifty, Sadia Basher, Abdullah Al Zayed, Mohammad Abrar Kabir, Rakibul Hasan Sagor

item.title: Voltage-Enhanced Photorefractive Hysteresis in Thin-Film Lithium Niobate Photonic-Crystal Cavities
item.description: arXiv:2611.34919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We observe voltage-enhanced photorefractive hysteresis in thin-film lithium niobate nanocavities, causing the resonance to appear at different wavelengths during increasing- and decreasing-wavelength laser scans. Their separation grows with bias magnitude and optical power, but depends weakly on scan speed over 1-200 nm/s. A quasi-static surface-trap model links voltage-biased carrier transport to asymmetric trapping, whose space-charge field shifts the resonance through the Pockels effect. The model captures this hysteresis across three cavities through switching between stable steady states. Space-charge feedback opposes further carrier separation, limiting the hysteresis gap. The model informs photorefractive mitigation and resonance control in integrated electro-optic devices.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Buzzi, Bjarke A. Frederiksen, Mikkel Heuck, Dirk R. Englund, Dashiell L. P. Vitullo

item.title: Infrared-absorption magnetometry in a diamond nanocavity: demonstration and limits at the nanoscale
item.description: arXiv:2611.33481v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diamond quantum sensors promise both high spatial resolution and high sensitivity; however, conventional photoluminescence-based spin readout can be difficult to integrate efficiently. Infrared absorption by nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond provides a promising alternative, although the sensitivity of compact absorption-based sensors is limited by the short optical interaction length between the probe field and the NV ensemble. To overcome this limitation, we demonstrate, for the first time, singlet-absorption magnetometry using spin-dense diamond nanocavities. By probing cavity modes near the 1042 nm NV singlet transition, we observe spin-dependent cavity transmission and perform cavity-enhanced magnetic field sensing. We further develop and experimentally validate a model that accurately predicts the spin-dependent cavity response, describes the optimal operating conditions, and identifies the practical limitations of different optically detected magnetic resonance modalities. Together, these results establish cavity-enhanced singlet absorption as a scalable readout mechanism for integrated diamond quantum sensors and provide a practical framework for engineering next-generation nanophotonic diamond quantum magnetometers.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas J. Sorensen, Elham Zohari, Chris Coutts, Sean McNaney, Matteo Feder, Hadi Zadeh-Haghighi, Sigurd Fl{\aa}gan, Vinaya K. Kavatamane, Christoph Simon, Paul E. Barclay

item.title: On-Demand Tailoring of High-Dimensional Orbital Angular Momentum States via a Phase-Only Hologram
item.description: arXiv:2611.33704v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Photonic orbital angular momentum (OAM) provides a naturally discrete and unbounded Hilbert space for high-dimensional encoding and has emerged as a powerful degree of freedom for advanced information processing. On-demand tailoring of both the amplitude and phase profiles of high-dimensional OAM states is essential for numerous applications, particularly in quantum information science. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate an efficient method for achieving such on-demand tailoring using a purely phase-only modulation scheme. The measured fidelity remains above 80% even for a 128-dimensional state, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Compared with previous techniques, our method achieves significantly higher generation efficiency, and this advantage becomes more pronounced as the dimensionality increases. Moreover, our approach substantially reduces experimental complexity while maintaining precise control, thereby offering a practical and scalable solution for high-dimensional OAM state engineering in both classical and quantum information processing.
item.dc:creator: Hao Sheng, Zi-Shuo Wang, Sheng-Qiang Jia, Zi-Mo Cheng, Li Fan, Jianping Ding, Jia-Min Xu, Zhi-Cheng Ren, Xi-Lin Wang, Hui-Tian Wang

item.title: When Malus' Law Meets the Wigner-Bell Inequality: Violation by Nonseparable Classical Light
item.description: arXiv:2611.33729v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bell-type inequalities are commonly associated with quantum nonlocality, yet their mathematical structure also reflects more general constraints on the joint probability distributions assigned to measurements performed in different contexts. Here we examine this distinction through the Wigner--Bell inequality using a classical optical field with two nonseparable degrees of freedom. Starting from a subsystem response-factorization assumption, we derive a Wigner-type probability bound requiring the pairwise measurement statistics to be compatible with a single nonnegative global joint distribution. For a classically nonseparable optical field, the corresponding joint probabilities are represented directly by normalized joint intensities and obey Malus' law. We show that these Malus-law probabilities violate the Wigner--Bell bound over a finite range of analyzer settings. The violation does not imply spatial nonlocality or a failure of classical electrodynamics. Rather, it demonstrates the incompatibility of context-dependent optical projection statistics with the global probability assignment underlying the Wigner construction. We further derive an extended Wigner-Bell bound for general imperfect correlations and propose an interferometric experiment for reconstructing the required joint probabilities from intensity measurements. These results provide a transparent optical realization of the probabilistic structure behind Bell-type inequalities and help distinguish consequences of Hilbert-space structure, nonseparability, and measurement context from those specifically associated with quantum nonlocality.
item.dc:creator: Xiao-Feng Qian

item.title: A bright source of high-dimensional spatially entangled photon pairs based on beam-like Type-II SPDC
item.description: arXiv:2611.33852v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bright sources of high-dimensional spatially entangled photon pairs are increasingly required for the rapid advancement of quantum technologies. However, simultaneously achieving high brightness and high-dimensional spatial entanglement through spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate a bright source of high-dimensional spatially entangled photon pairs using beam-like Type-II SPDC in a $\beta$-barium borate crystal. Compared with a conventional collinear Type-I source, it exhibits a $\sim$1.56-fold enhancement in the detected single-photon count rate and a $\sim$1.45-fold enhancement in the coincidence count rate. Measurements of position correlations and momentum anti-correlations certify at least 62-dimensional spatial entanglement within a 121-dimensional basis. These correlations are further exploited to demonstrate quantum imaging in both the position and momentum domains. These characteristics make the source a practical resource for high-dimensional photonic quantum technologies.
item.dc:creator: Ming Zhang, Zhiming Qing, Zhi-Cheng Ren, Jianping Ding, Xi-Lin Wang, Hui-Tian Wang

item.title: Why do single photons produce interference fringes? The phase of a mode and the phase of a state
item.description: arXiv:2611.34554v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: If the phase of a photon-number state is completely undetermined, how can single photons, sent one at a time through a two-slit apparatus, build up interference fringes? These lecture notes answer this question from first principles. Starting from Maxwell's equations, we expand the field in vector modes, quantize it, and introduce the quantity measured by a photodetector. We then show that the word ``phase'' refers to two different things: the phase of a mode, fixed by the optical setup, and the phase of the quantum state that excites the mode. Only the first determines the fringes. All calculations are given in full, and problems with solutions are included.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Aiello

item.title: Transition Path Sampling for Rare Events in Non-Markovian Open Quantum Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.34883v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rare transitions govern the dynamics of many open quantum systems, but their probabilities and rates are difficult to calculate. Transition path sampling (TPS) of quantum systems has so far been limited to Markovian, perturbative descriptions. Here, we formulate TPS for non-Markovian quantum state diffusion, which is exact for Gaussian baths, extending it to non-Markovian and strongly coupled open quantum systems. For normal-to-superradiant tunneling in the unbalanced open Dicke model, we determine probabilities down to $10^{-8}$ and rates beyond the reach of brute force.
item.dc:creator: Ritesh Pant, Kai M\"uller, Tarun Gera, Doran I. G. B. Raccah

item.title: Autonomous frequency locking for zero-offset microcomb
item.description: arXiv:2403.02868v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Stabilization of carrier-envelop-offset frequency ($f_{\mathrm{ceo}}$) in a microcomb typically relies on an additional optical or microwave reference. Here we propose autonomous frequency locking, in which Kerr comb formation and quadratic frequency conversion cooperate within a single microcavity to establish a zero-offset comb from one continuous-wave pump. The internal second-order interaction supplies phase-sensitive feedback that pins $f_{\mathrm{ceo}}$ to zero while the repetition rate self-adjusts to an integer division of the pump frequency. A second-order Adler-type equation links the locking threshold to the $\chi^{(2)}$ coupling strength and modal photon numbers. Simulations support this prediction and demonstrate recovery of the locked phase after perturbation. To explore a minimal realization of this mechanism, we further analyze a three-mode $\chi^{(3)}$ optical parametric oscillator whose signal and idler fields are coupled through $\chi^{(2)}$ conversion. Together, these interactions lock the signal and idler fields to $2/3$ and $4/3$ of the pump frequency. This configuration enables fractional-harmonic synthesis and provides a zero-offset frequency grid for measuring $f_{\mathrm{ceo}}$ with only one-third-octave spectral coverage. Our results establish internal frequency conversion as a route to autonomous microcomb control.
item.dc:creator: Fengyan Yang, Ming Li, Juanjuan Lu, Guang-Can Guo, Chang-Ling Zou

item.title: Lossless propagation of gain-compensated graphene plasmons
item.description: arXiv:2603.21274v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Graphene plasmons offer strong electromagnetic confinement and electrical tunability, but dissipation in the graphene sheet limits their propagation. Here, we investigate how optical gain in the surrounding dielectrics can compensate these losses in single- and double-layer graphene. Starting from the full electromagnetic boundary conditions and a finite-temperature graphene conductivity, we derive the compensation condition for a single sheet and the separate optical and acoustic dispersion relations for two coupled sheets. We show that the required gain depends both on material loss and on where the gain is placed. When gain is present throughout the dielectric environment, the two double-layer modes have nearly identical compensation thresholds. When it is confined to the spacer or the outer claddings, their thresholds separate because the modes overlap differently with each region. Full-wave finite-element simulations reproduce the predicted branches and field symmetries and show a strong suppression of attenuation together with a substantial increase in propagation length. The analysis also identifies the range over which a local conductivity provides a controlled description. These results show how the spatial distribution of gain can be used to control the compensation thresholds of the optical and acoustic graphene plasmons.
item.dc:creator: Andrianos Sygrimis, Giorgos P. Tsironis

item.title: Anisotropy in Fourier space optical memory effect correlations
item.description: arXiv:2605.03469v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate anisotropy in Fourier-domain speckle correlations associated with the optical memory effect in disordered scattering media. Within a single scattering framework, we show that while the conventional memory effect constrains transverse wavevector shifts, the correlation strength also depends non-trivially on differences in the axial wavevector components. Our theory is supported by numerical simulations of a three-dimensional, single scattering medium, which show excellent agreement with theory. We extend the analysis to pseudo-correlations, demonstrating that analogous anisotropic behavior arises in the conjugate memory effect. Our results highlight the often overlooked role of axial disorder in scattered field correlations.
item.dc:creator: Niall Byrnes, Matthew R. Foreman

item.title: Multi-pulse accumulation of gas molecular coherence enables gigahertz ultrafast frequency conversion
item.description: arXiv:2606.11811v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Frequency conversion of ultrafast lasers is fundamentally constrained by the trade-off between pulse energy and repetition rate. Here, we demonstrate a frequency conversion mechanism in which molecular coherence accumulates across ultrafast pulse trains in gas-filled hollow-core fibers. Unlike conventional nonlinear interactions initiated by individual high-energy pulses, this mechanism relies on the collective buildup of coherent molecular oscillations driven by successive pulses. Using this approach, we achieve Raman frequency conversion at repetition rates up to 3 GHz with nanojoule pulse energies. The results demonstrate that accumulated molecular coherence can govern nonlinear frequency conversion, revealing a domain of light-matter interaction whose physical limits remain largely unexplored.

item.title: Dynamics of confined acoustic phonon modes in nanocrystalline silicon membranes
item.description: arXiv:2607.14417v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We report femtosecond time-resolved measurements of confined acoustic phonons in free-standing nanocrystalline silicon membranes and compare them with the crystalline silicon counterpart. While the latter exhibits well-resolved higher-order modes, a strong suppression of these modes is observed in nanocrystalline samples. The suppression is strongly frequency dependent and becomes more pronounced at shorter phonon wavelengths, consistent with stronger scattering by the nanocrystalline microstructure. Analysis of the phonon lifetimes reveals an additional frequency-dependent scattering mechanism in nanocrystalline silicon, with a scattering rate that scales approximately as $f^2$, where $f$ is the phonon frequency. The measured sound velocity is consistent with previous reports for nanocrystalline silicon and indicates an effective elastic response arising from multiple crystallographic orientations. These results establish coherent phonons as a sensitive probe of microstructure-dependent scattering in nanocrystalline materials and indicate that grain boundaries act as an effective spectral filter for high-frequency acoustic phonons.
item.dc:creator: Tiago E. C. Magalh\~aes, T\^ania M. Ribeiro, Oili M. E. Ylivaara, Jouni Ahopelto, Clivia M. Sotomayor Torres

item.title: Triple-Resonance Spectroscopy Using a Cavity-Enhanced Frequency Comb Probe
item.description: arXiv:2607.15793v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurate experimentally verified models of molecular hot-band transitions are essential for interpreting high-temperature spectra in environments ranging from exoplanetary atmospheres to combustion systems. However, line-resolved measurements of infrared hot-band transitions reaching highly excited vibrational states above 10000 cm$^{-1}$ are missing because these transitions are too weak to observe at room temperature and the spectra are congested at elevated temperatures. Here, we introduce a nonlinear spectroscopic approach that enables simultaneous measurement of individual infrared hot-band transitions between four vibrational bands up to 12000 cm$^{-1}$ over a broad spectral range with Doppler-free resolution and sub-MHz frequency accuracy (10$^{-10}$ relative line position accuracy). The method is based on an all-optical triple-resonance (AOTR) scheme that combines stepwise mid-infrared pumping using an optical-frequency-comb-stabilized, double-seeded continuous-wave optical parametric oscillator with broadband highly sensitive near-infrared probing using a cavity-enhanced optical frequency comb. As a proof of principle, we measure transitions between high polyads (P) of methane - groups of strongly interacting, near-degenerate vibrational energy states arising from couplings between the C-H stretching and bending modes. In the probe spectra, we simultaneously resolve Doppler-free P4$\leftarrow$P0, P6$\leftarrow$P2 and P8$\leftarrow$P4 transitions, reaching the poorly understood polyad P8 near 12000 cm$^{-1}$ and providing the first set of 105 experimentally observed lines in the P8$\leftarrow$P4 spectral region, of which 39 lines are assigned, reaching 24 unique final states. Comb-based AOTR spectroscopy opens a new route for broadband exploration of highly excited molecular states, delivering extensive high-accuracy spectroscopic data needed to refine molecular models.
item.dc:creator: Qinxue Nie, Vinicius Silva de Oliveira, Adrian Hj\"alt\'en, Isak Silander, Kevin K. Lehmann, Aleksandra Foltynowicz

item.title: Quantized response of amplification in non-Hermitian photonic time quasicrystals
item.description: arXiv:2609.24327v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Photonic time crystals amplify waves through periodic temporal modulation of the permittivity. We study a non-Hermitian photonic time quasicrystal, a temporal analogue of the non-Hermitian Aubry-Andre-Harper model of quasiperiodic lattices. Its modulation is incommensurate and has a complex phase, whose imaginary part, the complexification parameter, acts as an imaginary gauge field on the modulation harmonics. We find that the bulk amplification rate, as a function of this parameter, is organized into distinct phases, within each of which its slope is locked to an integer, known in quasiperiodic operator theory as Avila's acceleration. The phase boundaries are predicted from Fourier coefficients of rational approximants and confirmed by transfer-matrix and time-domain simulations. Under analytic distortions of the modulation waveform, the integer phases persist while their boundaries move. Consequently, two input frequencies in different integer phases have an amplification ratio that varies exponentially with the complexification parameter, which enables spectral selection. These results establish a topologically protected, quantized response law for amplification in such time-varying media.
item.dc:creator: Shuhang Chen, Zhi Zheng, Qi Zhu

item.title: DUV (257 nm) LIDT of Anti-Reflective Coatings
item.description: arXiv:2611.26181v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Laser-induced damage threshold in the deep ultraviolet (DUV) was used to perform tests on AR coated windows intended for industrial processes. The 257 nm wavelength was generated from Yb:YAG fundamental (1030 nm) and the long-term LIDT stability (up to 100000 shots) was selected as representative for minimal industrial qualification. Selected setup for the fourth harmonics generation consists of two stages, generation of second harmonic and subsequently the fourth harmonic with 13,4% conversation efficiency. In both 1-on-1 and S-on-1 experiments, the optics coated with Al2O3/SiO2 by ion beam sputtering technique demonstrated the highest LIDT value of 0.73 and 0.5 J/cm2 respectively. Various damage morphologies, color centers, ballistic damage, delamination, and blistering were observed across the samples with respect to the 1-on-1 and S-on-1.

item.title: Dark and bright solitons in a multimodal lithium tantalate microresonator
item.description: arXiv:2611.30313v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bright-soliton and dark-pulse microcombs provide complementary outputs. Integrating both states in a single resonator would expand the operating capabilities of an integrated coherent source, but requires opposite group-velocity-dispersion (GVD) channels while reconciling localized interfamily interaction for dark-pulse formation with spectral isolation for independent bright-soliton pumping. Wavelength-addressed access to both states is achieved in a LiTaO$_3$ microring through two TE-like transverse mode families. The higher-order TE$_{10}$ family fulfills two distinct roles in different spectral regions. Within localized avoided-mode-crossing regions, mode-resolved spectroscopy implicates TE$_{10}$ in perturbing the normal-GVD TE$_{00}$ resonance sequence. Away from these regions, TE$_{10}$ retains anomalous GVD and remains spectrally isolated as an independently pumpable bright-soliton channel; at representative pump resonances, the closest resonance of the non-addressed family is separated by 75--192 loaded cavity linewidths. With the input polarization held fixed, pumping TE$_{00}$ and TE$_{10}$ resonances generates dark-pulse and bright-soliton microcombs, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first experimental realization of a dark-pulse microcomb in an integrated LiTaO$_3$ microring. These results establish transverse-mode-family engineering as a route to combining localized modal interaction with independent spectral addressing in a single microresonator.
item.dc:creator: Huizong Zhu, Yuyao Guo, Xiangfei Cheng, Yiqun Wu, Juanjuan Lu

item.title: Multiscale Numerical Modelling of Ultrafast Laser-Matter Interactions: Maxwell Two Temperature Model Molecular Dynamics (M-TTM-MD)
item.description: arXiv:2601.20763v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this work, we present a comprehensive numerical framework that couples numerical solutions of Maxwell's equations using the Finite-Difference Time-Domain (FDTD) approach, Molecular Dynamics (MD), and the Two-Temperature Model (TTM) to describe ultrafast laser-matter interactions in metallic systems at the atomic scale. The proposed Maxwell-Two-Temperature Model-Molecular Dynamics (M-TTM-MD) bridges the gap between electromagnetic field propagation, electron-phonon energy exchange, and atomic motion, allowing for a self-consistent treatment of energy absorption, transport, and structural response within a unified simulation environment. The calculated electromagnetic fields incorporate dispersive dielectric properties derived using the Auxiliary Differential Equation (ADE) technique, while the electronic and lattice subsystems are dynamically coupled through spatially and temporally resolved energy exchange terms. The changes in the material topography are then reflected in the updated grid for the FDTD scheme. The developed M-TTM-MD model provides a self-consistent numerical framework that offers insights into laser-induced phenomena in metals, including energy transport and surface dynamics under extreme nonequilibrium conditions.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Comput. Phys. Commun., vol. 332, Art. no. 110518, 2026

item.title: A van der Waals photon-ratchet for enhancing spin defect emission and quantum sensing
item.description: arXiv:2602.02256v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Spin defects in two-dimensional materials are promising platforms for quantum information technologies and nanoscale sensing. The negatively charged boron vacancy (VB-) in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is particularly attractive due to its sensitivity to temperature, magnetic fields, and pressure, but its application is limited by intrinsically weak photoluminescence (PL). Here we demonstrate a van der Waals heterostructure that enhances the PL intensity of VB- by up to 45x at 4 Kelvin while preserving compatibility with ultrathin optoelectronic platforms. A type-I band alignment at the PbI2-hBN interface facilitates efficient interlayer coupling to the defect, and strong spectral overlap supports fluorescence resonance energy transfer. Ab initio calculations indicate that this coupling enables a photon-ratcheting mechanism, in which optical absorption in PbI2 generates a nonlinear polarization that drives VB- excitation. This process is consistent with interlayer energy transfer while maintaining minimal electronic and spin hybridization and preserving optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) contrast. The heterostructure further exhibits improved sensitivity to external magnetic fields. These results establish a route for the enhancement of defect emission via interlayer optical coupling and introduce a general materials strategy for amplifying weak quantum defect signals in nanomaterials.
item.dc:creator: Eveline Mayner, Yaroslav Zhumagulov, Cristian de Giorgio, Feihong Chu, Prabhu Swain, Georg Fantner, Andras Kis, Oleg Yazyev, Aleksandra Radenovic

item.title: A Framework for Closed-Loop Robotic Assembly, Alignment and Self-Recovery of Precision Optical Systems
item.description: arXiv:2603.21496v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robotic automation has transformed scientific workflows in domains such as chemistry and materials science, yet free-space optics, which is a high-precision domain, remains largely manual. Optical systems impose strict spatial and angular tolerances, and their performance is governed by tightly coupled physical parameters, making generalizable automation particularly challenging. In this work, we present a robotics framework for the autonomous construction, alignment, and maintenance of precision optical systems. Our approach integrates a hierarchical computer vision system, optimization routines, and custom-built tools to achieve this functionality. As a representative demonstration, we perform the fully autonomous construction of a tabletop laser cavity from randomly distributed components. The system performs several tasks such as laser beam centering, spatial alignment of multiple beams, resonator alignment, laser mode selection, and self-recovery from induced misalignment and disturbances. By achieving closed-loop autonomy for highly sensitive optical systems, this work establishes a foundation for autonomous optical experiments for applications across scientific domains.
item.dc:creator: Seou Choi, Sachin Vaidya, Caio Silva, Shiekh Zia Uddin, Sajib Biswas Shuvo, Shrish Choudhary, Marin Solja\v{c}i\'c

item.title: Time Interfaces Enable Free-Space Excitation of Frozen Electromagnetic Waves and Topological Edge States in Graphene
item.description: arXiv:2611.26714v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Time-varying two-dimensional materials, such as graphene under ultrafast photoexcitation, offer a promising platform for engineering temporal interfaces for electromagnetic waves. Rapidly promoting valence electrons to the conduction band generates a high-energy, non-thermal hot-electron population that subsequently thermalizes with the pre-existing thermal electron population. We study the excitation of plasmonic modes in graphene by the time interface created by ultrafast photoexcitation using a graphene electron-transport model self-consistently coupled to electromagnetic simulations. We find that, in addition to dynamic, propagating plasmonic modes, the time interfaces excite static, spatially varying electromagnetic modes in the interaction region, sustained by streaming transverse electrons. We also demonstrate a novel technique for coupling free-space light directly to highly localized topological edge states at the magnetic-inversion boundary on graphene, eliminating the need for near-field excitation techniques.
item.dc:creator: Shivaksh Rawat, Samyobrata Mukherjee, Jeffery Allen, Monica Allen, Gennady Shvets
